# 16-pairio — sources

Back-test entry `16-pairio.yaml`: Pairio, a voice assistant that helps factory technicians fix broken machines (YC
Spring 2026, P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named
(the launch-era site is in German; its quotes are given in German, with the author's English in brackets). "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-04-21 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one
exists; anything later is marked as later).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Pairio – Fix broken equipment in factories faster", 2026-04-21 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Q18-pairio-fix-broken-equipment-in-factories-faster
- [WB] pairio.com as archived 2026-04-18, three days before launch (German) — https://web.archive.org/web/20260418031841/https://pairio.com/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/pairio
- [BLOG] Pairio blog, "the same problems at every plant" (a founder's six weeks of US plant visits), datePublished 2026-05-17 — https://pairio.com/blog/same-problems-every-plant-every-industry/
- [FAQ] pairio.com FAQ, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com/faq/
- [REF] pairio.com customer reference (Knipping), read 2026-10-22; figures "supplied by Knipping" — https://pairio.com/customer-references/
- [SITE] pairio.com, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers and millwrights, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/installation-maintenance-and-repair/industrial-machinery-mechanics-and-maintenance-workers-and-millwrights.htm

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Maintenance technicians and operators who fix machines on the production line.
   [LYC] "Pairio helps technicians and operators resolve faults faster with voice AI." [YCP] "AI mobile app that helps
   factory technicians fix broken machines". → `roles[technician]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: the
   technician only (operators are named too, but the fix and the report are the technician's).

2. **What (the job).** Get the machine running again fast, and keep the fix for the next person.
   [LYC] "Unplanned equipment downtime costs global industries over $1.4 trillion every year – and the root cause isn't
   broken machines. It's broken knowledge transfer." [LYC] "With the average technician in the US now 50 years old,
   knowledge is literally walking out the door". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the machine, when it fails, and afterwards when the fix should be written down.
   [LYC] "When a machine fails, resolution speed depends almost entirely on whether the one guy who's seen this before is
   working that day"; "Valuable technical clues are buried somewhere across 400 pages of OEM manuals or locked in outdated
   software"; "After spending 6 hours getting the line back up, the last thing a technician does is sit down and write a
   detailed fault report to institutionalize their knowledge". [FAQ] "Fundamentals and practical ways to use Pairio in
   day-to-day maintenance work." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: machine breakdown`. Author's choice: the window
   {5, WORKING_DAYS} (a working-day rhythm) and Frequency 2 to 4 working days out of 5 -- daily for the team, not for
   each technician (header); Prevalence `p_80_100`.

4. **Which people.** Technicians at US plants that keep their own maintenance team.
   [LYC] "Ask: Can you introduce us to plant and maintenance managers at US manufacturing firms?" [WB] "Pairio richtet sich
   an Unternehmen mit eigener Instandhaltung - vom Mittelstand bis zum Konzern." [Pairio is for companies with their own
   maintenance, from mid-sized firms to groups.] → `context.segment`, `market: US`; the German plants are in the header.

5. **Who pays.** The plant; the maintenance manager chooses, the plant manager agrees.
   [LYC] "If you know anyone in plant operations or maintenance in US manufacturing we'd love to talk with them". [WB]
   quotes a "Meister & Abteilungsleiter Instandhaltung" [foreman and head of maintenance] as a user. → `persona.
   decision_maker: {role: manager}`; Buyer and payer tests "The plant manager" (listed with "The IT department"):
   author's choice, no source names who signs. Purchase friction's tested item, "Connecting it to SAP or Maximo": [FAQ]
   "including systems such as SAP, IFS, IBM Maximo, Oracle EAM Cloud, Hexagon, SharePoint, Outlook, and Asset API"; [WB]
   "Die genaue Anbindung hängt von Ihrer IT-Landschaft ab." [The exact connection depends on your IT landscape.] The IT
   security review and the plant-wide rollout sign-off are the author's. Commitment's step, "run a pilot on one
   production line": [REF] "A clearly scoped pilot creates evidence"; "Following a two-month pilot, the solution was
   integrated in four weeks." (later than launch; the launch-era site offers "Kostenlose Demo" [free demo]).

6. **Mechanism.** Ask by voice or photo; answers from the manuals and past repairs; speak the fix, get a report.
   [LYC] "Simply ask and instantly receive any available technical clue"; "Speak and let Pairio structure their learnings
   into reusable know-how"; "Use photos and videos to capture even more contextual knowledge". [WB] "Sprache, Foto oder
   Video rein - fertiger Bericht raus" [voice, photo or video in, finished report out]; "Pairio erkennt Fehlerbild,
   Maßnahmen, Ersatzteile und erstellt einen strukturierten Bericht." [Pairio recognises the fault, the actions, the spare
   parts and writes a structured report.] [YCP] "Users just take a picture of the broken machine and we search thousands
   of pages of manuals to find the right solution." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (a phone
   allowed at the machine — tested; manuals as files; quiet enough to speak) and Adoption friction (speak the fix when
   done — tested; photograph the fault first) are the author's, from the mechanism's own needs and [BLOG] ("tools that fit
   how technicians actually work, on mobile, in loud environments"). Relative advantage: shorter_time from [WB] "-25%
   MTTR", less_help_needed from [LYC]'s "the one guy who's seen this before"; the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price public; the cost is technician time.
   [WB] "Kostenlose Demo" and "Demo buchen" [free demo; book a demo], no price; [SITE] "Book a free demo", no price.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $600 to $1,200 per technician a year is **the operator's reading** (about $50 to
   $100 a seat a month; header). Existing sacrifice, HOURS 150 to 300 of the breakdowns per technician a year: author's
   arithmetic -- 3 to 6 hours a week of a technician's time lost to hunting through manuals, waiting for the one person
   who knows, extra trips for tools and parts, and the report written afterwards, over about 50 working weeks; the scale
   is set by [LYC]'s "6 hours getting the line back up" and by [WB]'s "-25% MTTR" and "-80% Ablageaufwand" (the shares
   the company says it removes). The rate, $31 an hour, is [BLS] "$30.82 per hour" (May 2025 median), the author's
   stand-in. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [BLOG] "At a specialty manufacturer in Illinois, the maintenance team told me some shifts run with a single
   technician."; "The troubleshooting descriptions? Consistently useless. 'Reset machine.' 'Machine broken, fixed it.'
   'Called supplier.'"; "The work order says there's a problem with the injection molding machine. That's it. They show
   up, assess, go back for parts, come back again."; "When a conveyor goes down, every minute counts in a way that's
   directly visible to the customer."; "she'd watched a technician try to use ChatGPT out of desperation to solve a
   machine-specific problem."

The price split (5 of 7 at or above the reading) is the author's: no public figure says what share would pay. No
respondent carries the name of a customer, technician or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea. [SITE] (English, 2026-10-22) describes the same assistant (fault reports, manual search, data analysis, work
instructions) now aimed at US plants, with the Knipping reference: [REF] "Knipping reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) by
25%, generated €500K in savings through avoided downtime, and achieved a 95% adoption rate." and "Four German locations
are already onboarded." [FAQ] "In suitable use cases, MTTR can be reduced by up to 25%, filing effort by up to 80%, and
onboarding time by up to 90%." Price today: still not public ("Book a free demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price.** Nothing public at launch or today; the founder's price is the operator's reading (header, item 7), so the
  Price line measures that reading, not the company's price.
- **A per-plant money cost.** Only the global $1.4 trillion is public; the chain cost is the technicians' time instead
  (header).
- **The hours per technician a year.** The sources give one example (6 hours on one breakdown) and shares removed; the
  150 to 300 is the author's arithmetic.
- **A technician's hour.** [BLS]'s median stands in.
- **Who signs, and the purchase steps.** No source names the buyer above the maintenance manager; the plant manager, the
  IT department, the security review and the rollout sign-off are the author's (the SAP or Maximo connection is sourced).
- **How often one technician meets a breakdown.** "Day-to-day" is the team's rhythm; the 2 to 4 working days out of 5 is
  the author's.
- **First-person technician accounts.** No Launch HN or forum thread; the occasions are scripted from [BLOG] (the
  founder's own account of US visits) and [WB]'s two user quotes ("Mit der App kann ich alles direkt dokumentieren und
  muss mir keine Sorgen machen, dass ich etwas vergesse." [With the app I can document everything straight away and
  needn't worry about forgetting something.]).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The two answers say different things -- one would pay more for a proven downtime drop on a line, the other says downtime comes from old machines and missing parts and wouldn't pay for another app -- so leaving each on its own is how I'd read them, and no group exists that either belongs in.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; both answers speak to what the tool would be worth.

founder.order_why: The flow runs well from context to problem to idea to buyer, but 'How should managers answer?' (24) sits after the interviews are marked sent, when it belongs with the other study set-up in step 5.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and the same question; 20 (first real step, which for me is a pilot on one line) and 22 (Offer a pilot?) cover the same ground; 10 and 14 both ask who decides and who must agree, which 15-16 then check again.
founder.missing: No screen asks what a technician's hour is worth, though the cost I gave on 12 is in technician hours, not dollars, and the price on 13 is in dollars.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The 'One more thing' screen about what would take the time in buying sits between question 5 and question 6 of 6, so it interrupts the count, and it would read better right after the sign-off and SAP/Maximo questions or at the very end.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7 overlap: screen 6 asks how long connecting to SAP or Maximo would take, and screen 7 asks again what would take the time in buying, which for me is mostly that same integration and IT work plus the plant manager sign-off from screen 5.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How many technicians I have and how many would use it, and whether the plant's IT or security people would have to approve a new tool on the floor. Also missing is how Pairio would help my Tech 1s learn to fix things like a Tech 3, which is the main reason I'd pay for it.

screens.why2: "Who has to agree before they can buy" is how I'd say it myself, and the hint that "Nobody" counts makes it easy to answer on the first read.
screens.why3: I sell into plants every week, so I know the plant manager signs off and IT gets pulled in once we talk about connecting to SAP or Maximo.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box, and the one escape chip, "Leave this out of the study", makes sense for a step I might not want to test.
screens.why5: I typed "The plant manager; The IT department", but the belief Keel wrote only says the plant manager has to agree, so the IT department I named has been dropped.
screens.instead: Same question; the belief should read: The maintenance manager decides, and the plant manager and the IT department have to agree.

screens.why1: Right after I named who else has to agree, it makes sense to show me the full cast before Keel tests the buyer and payer line.
screens.why2: Maintenance technician, maintenance manager, plant manager and IT department are exactly the words we use in a US plant.
screens.why3: I know who sits in a plant's buying chain for maintenance software, because I sell to these people every week.
screens.why4: The plant manager and IT rows carry no part, while the first two say 'has the problem' and 'decides to buy', so I can't tell from the list that the plant manager has to agree or what IT does; the capitalisation is also uneven.
screens.why5: The belief keeps 'maintenance manager decides, plant manager agrees', but it drops the IT department I named alongside the plant manager, even though IT still shows as a row.
screens.instead: The people involved: maintenance technician · has the problem; maintenance manager · decides to buy; plant manager · has to agree; IT department · has to approve the connection (SAP/Maximo).

screens.why1: Right after I named the plant manager and IT as the ones who must agree, it makes sense to pick which of the two to put to maintenance managers.
screens.why2: The list is plain, but the intro needs a second read: 'the person who decides gets one question… nothing is reworded here' is Keel talking about itself, not anything I'd say.
screens.why3: I know how a plant buys: the maintenance manager picks the tool, and the plant manager signs off on spend, so I can choose without guessing.
screens.why4: Plant manager, IT, and 'Nobody else' cover what I typed, are distinct, and the escape fits the case where the maintenance manager buys alone.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my roles, but the bar asks about the last time they bought 'something that keeps fault knowledge from walking out', and most US maintenance managers have never bought such a thing, so the test should ask about their last maintenance software or CMMS purchase.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? The plant manager / The IT department / Nobody else. Bar: holds if at least 2 in 3 maintenance managers say the plant manager had to sign off the last time they bought maintenance software for the plant.

screens.why1: Right after settling who pays and who must agree, asking what slows or stops the purchase is the natural next step in how it sells.
screens.why2: Approvals, reviews, procurement and switching are everyday words for me as a founder selling into plant maintenance, and the hint makes the 25-word answer easy.
screens.why3: I know the blockers from my own sales: the SAP or Maximo connection, the IT security review and the sign-off for a plant-wide rollout.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with one escape chip, and 'Leave this out of the study' is the right way out if I would rather not test friction.
screens.why5: Keel's belief keeps only my first friction, drops the IT security review and the rollout sign-off, and adds an 'about 6 weeks, or not need it' threshold I never typed.
screens.instead: Keep the same question, but write the belief from all three things I typed with no invented deadline: 'Most maintenance managers could get it connected to SAP or Maximo, through an IT security review and signed off for a plant-wide rollout.'

screens.why1: It follows straight from my answer on what could slow a purchase, so checking the list Keel drafted is the obvious next step before Keel tests it.
screens.why2: SAP, Maximo, an IT security review and a plant-wide rollout sign-off are everyday words to me and to any plant maintenance manager I sell to.
screens.why3: These are the exact hurdles I hit selling into plants: the CMMS or ERP hookup, IT security, and getting the rollout signed off after one line.
screens.why4: The three rows are distinct, in the buyer's own words, and cover the real hurdles; anything missing, like budget approval, I can add myself.
screens.why5: The rows are my words, and the belief tests the SAP or Maximo hookup in about 6 weeks or not at all, which matches how integrations actually go for us, with no leak to respondents.

screens.why1: Right after I named the three things that could slow a purchase, it is obvious that I now pick the one to test and say how long I expect it to take.
screens.why2: The options are my own words and SAP and Maximo are plain to me, but "how long would this step take before it went through" reads oddly for an integration, and the same hint is printed twice.
screens.why3: How long the SAP or Maximo hookup takes at a plant is something I deal with in every pilot, so 6 weeks is my own estimate to make.
screens.why4: The three steps are exactly the ones I listed, distinct and in my words, and the days, weeks and months menu covers how I would size it.
screens.why5: The belief says what I meant: most maintenance managers get the SAP or Maximo connection done within about 6 weeks, or do not need it.
screens.instead: Which step do you want to test? If they bought it, how long would this step take to get done? (Connecting it to SAP or Maximo / An IT security review / Sign-off for a plant-wide rollout), with the hint shown once.

screens.why1: Commitment comes right after who agrees and what could stop a purchase, so asking what first real step I want from the maintenance manager is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'First real step' plus the hint (time, data, money or a signature) is plain to me as a founder selling into plant maintenance, and 'pilot on one production line' is how my buyers talk.
screens.why3: What I ask a plant to commit to is my own sales motion, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a free-text commitment box, and nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my 'run a pilot on one production line', but adds 'now', which drifts a little: the pilot comes after a free demo, not on the spot.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want the maintenance manager to take? e.g. book a demo, then run a pilot on one production line

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step, it makes sense to show me how strangers will hear that step and how it will be tested before I move on.
screens.why2: "Pilot on one production line" is how any maintenance manager I'd talk to says it, and the bar of 1 in 3 saying probably not or no reads clearly on the first pass.
screens.why3: Whether a maintenance manager would put one line on a pilot is exactly the call those managers make, and it's the call I'm asking US plants to make.
screens.why4: The only choices are the drafted step and its bar, which I can keep or edit, and the step stays under the 9-word limit with nothing missing.
screens.why5: I typed "run a pilot on one production line", and the added "now" pushes it toward starting right away, even though I listed the SAP or Maximo hookup and the IT review as things that slow the start.
screens.instead: In most cases the maintenance manager would agree to run a pilot on one production line.

screens.why1: Right after I named my first step (a pilot on one production line), it makes sense to ask whether to invite the people who say yes before the study goes out.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is my own word for how plants buy, and the hint says exactly what strangers will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is my decision and nobody else's.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and both are worded the way I'd say them.
screens.why5: My step was 'run a pilot on one production line', but the line strangers see is a generic 'try this for real, leave your email', so the production-line pilot drops out of what the maintenance manager is asked.
screens.instead: Ask the managers who say yes if they'd run a pilot on one production line, and to leave their email? (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my technicians the questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says the interviewer is on video yet calls Daphne and Saskia voices, so I have to read it twice to work out whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both, and what the 400 credits buy.
screens.why3: I know my technicians are guys on a loud floor getting a text on their phone, so I can judge which interviewer they'd listen to.
screens.why4: Two interviewers to preview and pick from, with the preselected one marked, is complete and distinct, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: It keeps 'maintenance technicians' as I typed it and leaks nothing of Pairio to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should interview your maintenance technicians on video? (Daphne, picked for you ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s). 400 credits either way, and every question is also on screen to read and tap.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how technicians are interviewed, it makes sense to choose separately for the maintenance managers on the buying link before anything is sent.
screens.why2: The choice itself is plain, but the doubled "Daphne Daphne" and the status tags "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and "Ready when Daphne is" each need a second read to tell whether the video or the interviewer is the thing not ready.
screens.why3: I know my managers sit at desks and in planning meetings and would sooner tap through on a phone or laptop, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap and let-them-choose cover the real choices, don't overlap, and each says when it is ready, so I can see why Read and tap is the one available now.
screens.why5: It speaks of my managers as the respondents of the buying link and leaks nothing of Pairio to them, and Read and tap is what I picked.
screens.instead: How should maintenance managers answer? — Daphne asks aloud on video (ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap, and can speak or type into any box (ready now) / Let them pick when they open the link (ready once the video is)

screens.why1: The study is built and the links are sent, so the last thing I need to settle is who gets one; it belongs right at the end.
screens.why2: Plain to me as a founder: named people, a Keel contact search, or one open link posted where technicians already gather; only 'the Contacts page' leans on Keel's own layout, and the option explains it.
screens.why3: I know which plant and maintenance people I met on my six weeks of US visits and which ones I can reach, so I can answer this from what I actually have.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach people (by name, a found list, an open post), and none of them needs an escape chip.
screens.why5: My answer is kept, but the screen doesn't say whether it means the technicians' link, the managers' link from the screen before, or both, so I can't tell if my pick applies to both groups.
screens.instead: Who gets a link -- the maintenance technicians, and the maintenance managers? (for each: people I know by name / a list found with Keel / one open link posted where they already are)

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it: purchase friction, 3 of 7 expect longer than 6 weeks, against a bar of no more than 2 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The tally (4 holding, 1 did not hold, 1 too few, over 7 people) and each card's 'x of n · bar y of n · at the bar' make clear at first look what is counted, over how many, and where my bar sits.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the exact names and lines I checked on the way in: the maintenance manager decides with the plant manager agreeing, SAP or Maximo within about 6 weeks, and a pilot on one production line now.
screens.why_b4: The only sentence under the verdict says who the money questions went to; nothing says what a 6-week-to-3-month SAP/Maximo connection means for how I sell, such as a pilot that needs no integration or quoting a longer rollout.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible, at-the-bar results are only 'Holding up' and too few is said plainly, but the banner says every answer is the manager's while the sacrifice card reads '4 of 6 spend 150 hours', as if technicians had reported their own hours.
screens.instead: Did not hold on purchase friction: 3 of 7 managers expect the SAP/Maximo connection to take 6 weeks to 3 months, so offer a first-line pilot that runs without the integration and plan the rollout around a quarter, not six weeks.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "4 of 6 spend 150 hours or more · bar 4 of 6 · at the bar", so I see both the verdict and the count that decides it on first read.
screens.why_b2: The axis is labelled "hours of the breakdowns per technician a year", the strip shows 4 for and 2 against out of 6, and the marker reads "your bar · 4 of 6 (at least 2 in 3)", so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are all plain.
screens.why_b3: The belief line drops "per technician" ("spend 150 to 300 hours a year"), which on a manager's card could read as a team total; the verdict and bar line restore it, so it is recognisably mine but not quite how I wrote it.
screens.why_b4: "The cost is there… whether they would pay is the Price card, next" points me on but doesn't say what the 190-hour median, or the fact that it only cleared my low end and nobody went above 300, means for how I size the cost in my pitch.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says "a small group: a lean, not a call" and shows n, but "Holding up" and "The cost is there" read firmer than landing exactly on the bar with 4 of 6, where one answer the other way would flip it.
screens.instead: Just holding at the bar, 4 of 6 at or above 150 hours, median 190 and none above 300: a lean at the low end of your range, one answer from failing, so price against about 150 to 200 hours a technician, not 300.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 at $600 or more per technician a year · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I have the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The bands are yearly worth per technician, all 7 managers are plotted, and the bar at 5 of 7 is marked on both the chart and the strip, though my range label sitting on the $600–$1,000 band alone is slightly off since $1,200 crosses into the next band.
screens.why_b3: It is my price in my unit, $600 to $1,200 per technician a year, put to the maintenance managers I would sell to.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the count and sends me to Ability to pay; it never tells me what this means for my price, namely that the managers cluster at the low end of my range.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and "a lean, not a call" are shown, but "Holding up" for a $600–$1,200 belief overstates a bit: only 1 of the 5 went past $1,000, and the result sits exactly at the bar, so one answer would flip it.
screens.instead: Just at the bar, 5 of 7 at $600 or more, but 4 of those 5 sit under $1,000, so price toward $600 rather than $1,200; one answer either way flips this, and Mei-Ling would pay more once a line shows the downtime drop.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside its deciding number, 4 usable answers against the 5 needed, and the So line ties them together the same way.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts where the money would come from and puts the bar at 3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3), but the header's "4 answered" against the count line's "5 answered · 4 counted" took me a second look to see that Arturo is the grey cell.
screens.why_b3: The belief uses my $600 to $1,200 per technician a year, so I recognise it, but I never checked an Ability to pay line on the way in; Keel derived it from my price.
screens.why_b4: "Waits until 5 have" tells me I need one more manager to answer, but not what 3 of 4 from existing budget lines, and Darnell's multi-plant group needing a new line, mean for how I sell to plants.
screens.why_b5: With 4 counted it says "a lean, not a call" and withholds the verdict even though the count sits at the bar, so it claims nothing beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 managers who named your price would pay from a maintenance budget they already have, and only the multi-plant group would need a new line. That leans your way, but get one more answer, ideally from Arturo after his demo, before you count on it.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know my belief held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the seven managers' answers to the sign-off question, the strip shows 6 for and 1 against, and the marker sits at 5; the rule line explains why 'could sign alone' counts for me.
screens.why_b3: Both the name, Buyer and payer, and the line, the maintenance manager decides and the plant manager has to agree, are the ones I checked; the $600 in the question is my own price reading.
screens.why_b4: 'Plan for the plant manager in most deals' tells me concretely to bring the plant manager into the pilot pitch, and Darnell's quote under his row shows where that breaks.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line splits 5 as said from 1 easier, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a clean 6 of 7 from being sold as proof.
screens.instead: Plan for the plant manager in most deals; at multi-plant groups, expect corporate engineering may choose the software instead (1 of 7).

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits directly over "3 of 7 expect longer than 6 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 7", so I see the verdict and that one answer over the bar decided it.
screens.why_b2: The bands and the 7 people read at once, but the bar appears as "no more than 2 of 7" against in the header and "5 of 7" for on the chart, with the marker at 5 and only 4 cells for, so I had to work out that these are the same bar.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and my line about getting through the SAP or Maximo connection within about 6 weeks, or not needing it, are word for word what I checked, though the bar line "You said connecting it to SAP or Maximo." reads like a broken sentence.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for an integration cycle of 6 weeks to 3 months rather than my 6, and points me to Insights for what eats the time, which I can act on in how I scope a pilot and price the integration.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and "a lean, not a call" are visible, but "most often 6 weeks to 3 months" is wrong: 2 to under 6 weeks also has 3, so it is a tie, and since my 6 weeks is that band's low edge the miss is one manager at the line, not a clear tendency to run long.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one: 3 of 7 expect 6 weeks to 3 months, as many as expect 2 to 6 weeks; plan pilots so the line can start before the SAP or Maximo hookup is done.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar", so I know the belief held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the seven managers' answers to the pilot question (5 yes, 1 probably not, 1 no), and the strip puts the bar marker at 5, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Commitment and the belief line is word for word the one I checked: the maintenance manager would run a pilot on one production line now.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is a concrete next step: take the five yeses and schedule the pilot on one line.
screens.why_b5: The count line says it is a small group and a lean, but the So line treats a hypothetical "if it were ready today" yes as bookable without saying the result sits exactly at the bar, where one manager changing their mind flips it.
screens.instead: 5 of 7 said they'd pilot a line if it were ready today, exactly at the bar, so one changed mind flips it; ask those five for a named line and a start date to turn the yes into a real commitment.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict with the deciding count and bar beside it: Purchase friction did not hold at 3 of 7 against a bar of no more than 2 of 7, and Price and Buyer and payer held at 5 of 7 and 6 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, including the SAP or Maximo connection within about 6 weeks and the maintenance manager deciding with the plant manager agreeing.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the failed integration line means for selling to US plants, such as scoping the pilot without the SAP or Maximo hookup or planning a longer integration, and the one line that failed has no answers to act on.
screens.why_b5: No figure is overstated and the at-the-bar holds are not called strong, but the count line '3 against · 0 asked their why here · 3 never saw it' leaves me unsure whether the three against are the three named, and Commitment, also held at the bar with two against, is missing from the screen without a word.
screens.why_b6: Darnell's corporate engineering choosing for every plant, Sabine's old machines and missing parts, and Mei-Ling's 'show me the downtime drop on one line' are new to me, but the line that failed, what makes the integration take longer than 6 weeks, has no quotes at all.
screens.instead: Under Purchase friction, say plainly that none of the 3 who expect longer than 6 weeks were asked why, and what to do about it (ask them, or scope the pilot to run before the SAP or Maximo connection); and show Commitment's 2 'probably not or no' answers, since that line held only at the bar.

screens.why1: An idea card fits the buying part of my link, but as the very first thing I hear it lands cold, with nothing about my crew or the last breakdown before it.
screens.why2: SAP, Maximo and SharePoint are everyday words to me, but 'voice-first mobile assistant' is sales talk, and 'Pairio, answers and a fault report' doesn't tell me what the thing is; I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: My techs chasing manuals and wiring diagrams at a down machine, and the fix never getting written up in the CMMS, is exactly my week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The meaning holds, but 'voice-first' is the builder's own pitch word, and the belief line repeats the how ('answers with the source... SAP, Maximo or SharePoint') instead of saying what it would change for me.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is long: the colon list 'symptoms, actions, spare parts' and 'SAP, Maximo or SharePoint' said twice are a mouthful, and the opening line doesn't say what Pairio is.
screens.instead: Imagine Pairio, a phone app your techs talk to at a down machine. They ask by voice or photo and it finds the answer in your manuals, wiring diagrams and past repairs, and shows where it came from. When they're done, they say or show what they did, and it writes the work order into SAP, Maximo or SharePoint. The people building it believe it would get machines back up faster and leave a real record of every fix.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking what breakdowns cost my team in time makes sense before any talk of buying.
screens.why2: 'The breakdowns' points back to no breakdowns I was told about, and 'per technician' makes me divide in my head before I can answer.
screens.why3: I know our downtime and work-order hours roughly, but hours per tech for a whole year is a number I'd have to guess at from the CMMS.
screens.why4: The number box is fine, but 'None' next to 'I can't recall' is a second escape, and it overlaps with just typing 0.
screens.why5: It drifts from the job of getting a machine back up and recording the fix to all breakdown hours, which is a much bigger bucket than the time the idea would save.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clipped mouthful that you only follow by reading it.
screens.instead: Think of the last machine that went down on your line. About how many hours did your techs spend getting it running again? Type a number of hours, or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and a question about breakdown hours, asking what it would be worth to me per tech per year is the obvious next thing for the person who pays for the tools.
screens.why2: Price per technician per year is how I already budget for CMMS seats and training, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I sign off on tool spend for my team, so I know what I'd put against a seat like this.
screens.why4: The bands run cleanly with no overlap, cover what I'd plausibly spend per tech, and offer 'I wouldn't pay' and 'I can't say' as fair outs.
screens.why5: 'Answers and a fault report' is thin enough that I'm pricing a vague idea, so it may have drifted a little from what the founder meant, though nothing leaks.
screens.why6: The two-step bands say well, but 'Or say you can't say' is a clumsy line to hear and trips the ear.
screens.instead: What would Pairio be worth to you a year, per technician? Under $600; $600 to under $1,000; $1,000 or more; or you wouldn't pay for this. Or say: I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on it, asking where that money would actually come from is the obvious next step for someone who signs off on tools.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off, taken from other spending: that's how I talk about my maintenance budget, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I run the maintenance budget, so I know whether this would come out of our existing tools/MRO line, need a new line, or get robbed from parts or contractors.
screens.why4: The options switch to past tense ('we already had', 'someone signed off', 'there was no budget') for a 'would' question, and 'There was no budget for it' reads oddly after I just said I'd pay something; it means 'it wouldn't get funded' and should say so.
screens.why5: My answer was per technician a year, but the echo says just '$600 to $1,000 a year', which makes it sound like the whole team's cost and drifts from what I gave.
screens.why6: Short and holdable as a list of four, but 'Or say you can't say' trips on the ear and the tense mix stands out when heard.
screens.instead: You said about $600 to $1,000 a year per technician. If you went ahead at that, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have · A new budget line someone would sign off · Taken from other spending · It wouldn't get funded · (I can't say)

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price and said where the money would come from, it makes sense to ask whether I can approve it myself or need the plant manager.
screens.why2: Sign off and plant manager are everyday words in my job, and it asks one clear thing.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I can approve on my own budget and when I have to go to the plant manager.
screens.why4: The four cover my real answers, but putting the No answers before Yes reads oddly, and several people could include the plant manager.
screens.why5: It stays on my own buying authority at the price I gave, with nothing about the founder's plan leaking through.
screens.why6: The question and four options say well, but ending with 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy out loud.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about $600 per technician a year yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself · No, the plant manager would have to agree · No, several people would have to agree · No, it's someone else's decision · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I can sign off myself, asking what else has to happen before it is live is the natural next step in a buying decision.
screens.why2: SAP and Maximo are plain to me, but "connecting it ... before it went through" mixes up an approval with an integration job, so I'd read it twice to work out whether you mean IT approving it or the hookup actually working.
screens.why3: I know roughly how slow our IT and corporate are with anything touching the CMMS, but I'd be guessing at an integration time, and plenty of plants like mine run eMaint, Fiix or UpKeep rather than SAP or Maximo.
screens.why4: The time bands are clean and don't overlap, but there is no "we don't use SAP or Maximo" option, and "It wouldn't be needed" doesn't quite say that.
screens.why5: Naming SAP or Maximo as the step reads like the founder's own integration plan dropped in, and "before it went through" reads like a purchase step stretched over a technical one, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is one question with four short options, then a two-choice follow-up, and "SAP or Maximo" says fine, so I could answer it on one hearing.
screens.instead: If you bought Pairio, how long would it take to get it hooked into your CMMS? Under 2 weeks · 2 to under 6 weeks · 6 weeks to 3 months · 3 to 6 months · Over 6 months · We wouldn't hook it in; escape: I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after I said hooking it into Maximo would take a while, it makes sense to ask what would actually slow it down.
screens.why2: Short and plain, I can answer it straight off.
screens.why3: I know exactly what drags this out at my plant: IT security review, getting the CMMS admin's time, and corporate sign-off on anything touching SAP.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, so there are no options.
screens.why5: The last screen was about connecting it to SAP or Maximo, but this asks about buying it in general, so the step I was just thinking of has drifted a bit.
screens.why6: One short question that's easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would take the time in connecting Pairio to SAP or Maximo?

screens.why1: After the price, the payer, the sign-off and the SAP or Maximo hookup, the last thing to ask me is whether I'd actually try it, so this is the right spot to close on.
screens.why2: Running a pilot on one line is how I'd put any new tool in front of my techs, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: Whether to pilot a tool with my crew is my call and my budget, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: There's a 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes', so a cautious yes, which is where I'd likely land before seeing it work on our machines, has nowhere to go except a flat 'Yes'.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the card line 'answers and a fault report' doesn't tell me what Pairio is or who it's for, so I'm committing on a fuzzy picture.
screens.why6: One short question with three options read as a list I can hold after hearing them once; nothing trips the ear.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you run a pilot on one production line, or not? Yes, I'd run a pilot · Probably yes · Probably not · No
